claims.text: A machine-learning model should incorporate differences in alloy melting temperatures when predicting melting temperature and other melting properties of high-entropy alloys.
Differences in melting temperature among high-entropy alloys can affect machine-learning prediction accuracy.
BCC metals exhibit a transition from an athermal plateau to strong temperature dependence.
In BCC high-entropy alloys, the transition from an athermal plateau to strong temperature dependence occurs at approximately 0.4–0.5 of the melting temperature.
Accounting for the BCC athermal-to-temperature-dependent transition will improve predictions of melting temperature and other melting properties.
The model should be trained on a diverse dataset of high-entropy alloys spanning different melting temperatures and structures.
The machine-learning model will learn relationships among alloy composition, structure, and melting temperature.
Learned composition–structure–melting-temperature relationships will enable predictions for unseen high-entropy alloys.
The proposed model will improve melting-temperature prediction accuracy relative to current high-entropy-alloy prediction capabilities.
The proposed model will improve the computational efficiency of melting-temperature prediction.
The model will predict other, unspecified melting properties more accurately and efficiently.
The model's validity is limited to high-entropy alloys with compositions and structures similar to those represented in its training data.
Prediction uncertainty may arise from complex relationships among composition, structure, and melting temperature.
Poor accuracy on alloys significantly different from the training data would demonstrate a lack of model generalizability.
Poor accuracy on alloys significantly different from the training data would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated validity boundary limits the model to alloys similar to the training data, but the proposed falsification test uses alloys significantly different from the training data and treats failure there as falsification. Failure outside the declared applicability domain would not decisively contradict the bounded hypothesis.
